## What the one-liner in the paper is doing

Line 84 of `sections/02_model.qmd` compresses the whole derivation into a single
clause:

> using $F_{\text{Gumbel}(\overline{\mu},1)}(c) = \exp(-e^{-(c-\overline{\mu})}) = \exp(e^{\overline{\mu}} \ln \alpha) = \alpha^{S}$ when $c = F^{-1}(\alpha) = -\ln(-\ln\alpha)$.

The claim being supported is

$$
\Pr(y_{it} = w) \;=\; \alpha_w^{\,S_{it}} \;-\; \alpha_{w-1}^{\,S_{it}}.
$$

Below it is unpacked into four steps. Subscripts $i,t$ are dropped throughout.

## Step 0. The ingredients

Three facts are already established before this point in the paper.

**(a) The standard Gumbel CDF.**
$$
F(z) = \exp\left(-e^{-z}\right).
$$

**(b) The consumer's purchase probability.** She knows $u^*$ but not $\eta_0$, so
from her seat
$$
p = \Pr(\eta_0 < u^* \mid u^*) = F(u^*),
$$
because $\eta_0 \sim \text{Gumbel}(0,1)$. This is `eq-purchprob`.

**(c) The researcher's view of $u^*$.** By Lemma 1(i),
$$
u^* \sim \text{Gumbel}(\overline{\mu}, 1),
\qquad
\overline{\mu} = \ln S,
\qquad
S = \sum_{j} e^{V_j},
$$
so the CDF of $u^*$ is $\exp\left(-e^{-(c-\overline{\mu})}\right)$. Note the
relation we will use repeatedly:
$$
e^{\overline{\mu}} = e^{\ln S} = S .
$$

The asymmetry is the whole point: **she** conditions on $u^*$ and is uncertain
only about $\eta_0$; **we** do not observe $u^*$ and treat it as random.

## Step 1. Invert $F$ to get the utility-scale cut points

The reporting rule is stated on the probability scale, $p \in [\alpha_{w-1}, \alpha_w)$,
but the distribution we know is the one for $u^*$. So we need the utility value
$c$ at which $p$ crosses $\alpha$. Set $\alpha = F(c)$ and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha &= \exp\left(-e^{-c}\right) \\
\ln \alpha &= -e^{-c} \\
-\ln \alpha &= e^{-c} \\
\ln(-\ln \alpha) &= -c \\
c &= -\ln(-\ln \alpha).
\end{aligned}
$$

So $F^{-1}(\alpha) = -\ln(-\ln\alpha)$, which is the second half of the paper's
clause. It is well defined for $\alpha \in (0,1)$: there $\ln\alpha < 0$, so
$-\ln\alpha > 0$ and its log exists.

Keep the third line. It is the substitution that does the work in Step 2:
$$
e^{-c} = -\ln \alpha .
$$

## Step 2. The key identity

Evaluate the **researcher's** CDF for $u^*$ at that cut point.

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_{\text{Gumbel}(\overline{\mu},1)}(c)
&= \exp\left(-e^{-(c-\overline{\mu})}\right)
&&\text{(c) above} \\[4pt]
&= \exp\left(-e^{\overline{\mu}} \, e^{-c}\right)
&&\text{split the exponent: } e^{-(c-\overline{\mu})} = e^{-c}e^{\overline{\mu}} \\[4pt]
&= \exp\left(-e^{\overline{\mu}} \cdot (-\ln\alpha)\right)
&&\text{substitute } e^{-c} = -\ln\alpha \text{ from Step 1} \\[4pt]
&= \exp\left(e^{\overline{\mu}} \ln \alpha\right)
&&\text{two minus signs cancel} \\[4pt]
&= \exp\left(S \ln \alpha\right)
&&e^{\overline{\mu}} = S \\[4pt]
&= \alpha^{S}.
&&\exp(S\ln\alpha) = \left(e^{\ln\alpha}\right)^{S}
\end{aligned}
$$

That is the entire trick. A Gumbel CDF evaluated at another Gumbel's inverse CDF
collapses to a power, and the exponent is the inclusive value.

The reason it works is that the Gumbel CDF is a double exponential. Shifting the
location by $\overline{\mu}$ multiplies the inner exponential by
$e^{\overline{\mu}}$, and multiplying the inside of $\exp(-e^{-z})$ by a constant
is the same as raising the whole CDF to that power.

## Step 3. From the interval to the probability

The reporting rule says $y = w$ exactly when $p \in [\alpha_{w-1}, \alpha_w)$.
Since $p = F(u^*)$ and $F$ is strictly increasing, we can pull the event back to
the utility scale without changing it:

$$
p \in [\alpha_{w-1}, \alpha_w)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
u^* \in \left[\,F^{-1}(\alpha_{w-1}),\; F^{-1}(\alpha_w)\,\right).
$$

An interval probability is a difference of CDFs, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pr(y = w)
&= \Pr\left(u^* < F^{-1}(\alpha_w)\right) - \Pr\left(u^* < F^{-1}(\alpha_{w-1})\right) \\[4pt]
&= F_{\text{Gumbel}(\overline{\mu},1)}\!\left(F^{-1}(\alpha_w)\right)
 - F_{\text{Gumbel}(\overline{\mu},1)}\!\left(F^{-1}(\alpha_{w-1})\right) \\[4pt]
&= \alpha_w^{\,S} - \alpha_{w-1}^{\,S}
&&\text{by Step 2, applied twice.}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Step 4. Sanity checks

**The ends behave.** $\alpha_0 = 0$ gives $\Pr(y=1) = \alpha_1^S$, and
$\alpha_W = 1$ gives $\Pr(y=W) = 1 - \alpha_{W-1}^{S}$.

**The probabilities sum to one.** The sum telescopes:
$$
\sum_{w=1}^{W}\left(\alpha_w^S - \alpha_{w-1}^S\right)
= \alpha_W^S - \alpha_0^S = 1 - 0 = 1 .
$$

**The comparative static is the one claimed in the text.** For any
$\alpha \in (0,1)$, $\alpha^S \to 0$ as $S \to \infty$. So an attractive set
drives the cumulative probabilities of every low category to zero and pushes mass
to the top. As $S \to 0$, $\alpha^S \to 1$ and the mass collects at the bottom.

## A reframing that makes the result obvious

Step 2 says more than the paper uses. Read it as a statement about $p$ itself:

$$
\Pr(p \le a) \;=\; \Pr\left(u^* \le F^{-1}(a)\right) \;=\; a^{S}
\qquad \text{for } a \in (0,1).
$$

But $a^{S}$ on $[0,1]$ is the CDF of a $\text{Beta}(S, 1)$ random variable. So
from the researcher's perspective:

> **The consumer's purchase probability is $\text{Beta}(S,1)$ distributed, with the
> inclusive value as the single shape parameter.**

Everything in `eq-modelA` is then just that Beta CDF differenced across the cut
points, and the model's behavior falls out of a familiar distribution. Two
consequences:

- $\operatorname{E}[p] = \dfrac{S}{S+1}$, the mean of a $\text{Beta}(S,1)$. This is
  the $\frac{S}{S+1}$ factor that appears in the footnote `[^toy-ep]`.
- That mean equals $\dfrac{S}{S+1} = \Lambda(\overline{\mu})$, which is exactly
  Model B's purchase probability at $\gamma = 0$ (see `eq-collapseB`). So the two
  models agree on *average* demand even though they distribute the ordinal mass
  differently. I have not checked whether the paper states this anywhere; it may
  be worth a sentence.

## Numerical verification

```{r}
#| message: false
set.seed(1)

F_gum  <- function(z) exp(-exp(-z))          # standard Gumbel CDF
Finv   <- function(a) -log(-log(a))          # its inverse
rgumbel <- function(n, mu = 0) mu - log(-log(runif(n)))

V     <- c(1.2, 0.4, -0.3)                   # deterministic utilities
S     <- sum(exp(V))
mubar <- log(S)
alpha <- c(0, 0.37, 0.87, 1)                 # cut points, W = 3

## Step 2 identity: Gumbel(mubar,1) CDF at Finv(alpha) equals alpha^S
lhs <- F_gum(Finv(alpha[2:3]) - mubar)
rhs <- alpha[2:3]^S
cat("Step 2 identity:\n"); print(rbind(lhs, rhs))

## Step 3 formula, and that it sums to one
pw <- diff(alpha^S)
cat("\nPr(y = w):", round(pw, 5), " sum =", sum(pw), "\n")

## Monte Carlo from the behavioral process, not the formula
N     <- 2e6
ustar <- rgumbel(N, mubar)
p     <- F_gum(ustar)
y     <- cut(p, breaks = alpha, right = FALSE, labels = FALSE)
cat("simulated  :", round(as.numeric(table(y)) / N, 5), "\n")
cat("analytic   :", round(pw, 5), "\n")

## The Beta(S, 1) reframing
cat("\nKS test of p against Beta(S,1): p-value =",
    round(ks.test(sample(p, 5000), "pbeta", S, 1)$p.value, 3), "\n")
cat("E[p] simulated:", round(mean(p), 5),
    " | S/(S+1):", round(S / (S + 1), 5),
    " | plogis(mubar):", round(plogis(mubar), 5), "\n")
```
